column1: # Rambling speech development set: long, unrehearsed captures, paired with a
# clean twin carrying the same content.
# Written 2026-09-11 for the gap the readable sets no longer cover. The five
# development sets sit at or near their ceilings (coordination 115/121, routed
# 74/84, framing 41/45) while the sealed everyday set routes 168/240 and the
# adversarial set 52/116. A set that almost everything passes has stopped
# discriminating, so development steered by those sets is steered by
# instruments that cannot see the remaining failures.
# Provenance, stated so it can be checked rather than trusted: every utterance
# below was written from scratch for this file. Nothing was copied from a
# sealed set, from `Docs/PipelineSweep/*.md`, or from any other corpus in this
# repository, and the finished file was compared against all three sealed sets
# with a character-scanning overlap check before it was committed. The
# `Docs/PipelineSweep/rambling.md` lane analysed 376 rambling captures in
# August; that corpus lived in an ignored scratch directory and is gone, which
# is the capability this file restores.
# NOT held out: these are for iteration. Read the failures, fix the layer, run
# it again.
# What this set asserts, so that it can be argued with
# The product contract says Today is for action and Memory is for knowledge
# worth finding later, and that a capture keeps the speaker's words. Four
# claims follow from that and are what this file labels:
#   1. Filler does not change meaning. "Buy milk" and "um, so, yeah, buy
#      milk" are the same instruction, so they must produce the same rows.
#      This is the whole point of a voice-first app: the person is talking,
#      not typing, and talking carries filler.
#   2. A false start is not content. A speaker who begins, stops, and begins
#      again has said one thing, not two.
#   3. Deliberation that arrives at a decision is the decision. "I could do X
#      or Y, no, Y" is one errand, Y — the alternatives are not errands and
#      must not become rows.
#   4. Length is not a licence to split. A single coherent thought stays one
#      row at eighty words, and a run of errands stays several rows at eighty
#      words. The failure modes are opposite and both are here.
# How the pairing works, and why it is the measurement
# Each `*-clean` row has a twin `*-rambling` row with the SAME id stem, the
# same expected destination and the same expected thought count: RB04C and
# RB04R are one capture written twice. **The `C`/`R` suffix is the pairing
# key**, so a row without one is a deliberate singleton (RB25, RB26, RB27) and
# not half of a dropped pair — an earlier draft had two guard pairs carrying no
# suffix, which a stem-pairing scorer would have silently discarded, and they
# were precisely the rows guarding against the fix the gap is meant to
# motivate. The clean twin is the control. Its rate
# is not the finding — the GAP between the two rates is, because it isolates
# what filler and disfluency cost, with content held fixed by construction.
# Read them as pairs. A clean family at 20/20 and its rambling twin at 11/20
# means nine captures the app understands when typed and loses when spoken,
# which is the product's whole risk. Two families failing equally means the
# content is wrong for both and the rambling is not what broke it.
# Do NOT quote a single number over this file. The clean rows are deliberately
# easy and would flatter any average taken across both halves.
# What this set cannot tell you, established by review on 2026-09-11
# 1. **Read the thought-count column, not the destination column.** 59 of the
#    73 rows want Today, so answering "Today" to everything scores 81% and the
#    destination twin gap is a ceiling effect. Count is what discriminates
#    here. A flat destination gap is NOT evidence that rambling does not hurt
#    routing; it is evidence this set cannot see routing.
# 2. **Seven pairs are trivially passable and are named so nobody counts them
#    twice.** In RB09-RB11 and RB13-RB16 the clean twin is a literal suffix of
#    its rambling twin, so "return the final clause" scores 7/7 on them and
#    produces a twin gap of zero — which is this instrument's signal for
#    "filler cost nothing". They stay, because real deliberation and real
#    restarts do end on the resolution and the rows are natural. RB12 and
#    RB33-RB36 are the antidote: the disfluency sits mid-utterance with a
#    committed errand in front of it, so the last-clause heuristic returns one
#    row where two are wanted. **Any result on `restart` or `decision` must be
#    read against those, not against the suffix rows.**
# 3. **RB16R leans on `honestly`**, which everyday's title hygiene deliberately
#    does not treat as filler because it is an ordinary word often enough that
#    flagging it manufactures failures. If a future change reads it as a filler
#    marker, this set rewards it and the everyday set punishes it. It is not
#    wrong, but it is the row nobody should cite as proof.
# 4. **The set is tilted toward finding boundaries**: roughly twice as many
#    long captures reward emitting two or more rows as punish it. The `coherent`
#    and `two-facts` rows are the counterweight and the honest fix is more
#    one-thought *contents*, not more guards over the same few.
# The guard families
# `coherent-*` rows must produce ONE row however long they get, and they are
# here because every fix that finds more boundaries threatens them. A run that
# improves the errand families and breaks these has not improved anything.
# Columns: id, utterance, family, expected_destination, expected_thoughts

column1: # --- Label corrections, 2026-09-11 19:17, recorded rather than quietly applied
# RB28 and RB30 (both twins) wanted 3 thoughts and now want 4. I miscounted
# when I wrote them: RB28 enumerates the contractor's visit, moving the bikes,
# the second quote and the deck boards, and RB30 the blood work, the follow up,
# the supplements and telling Mum. Four units each, by the same reading of the
# product contract the other rows use.
# This is the change a dataset author should be most suspicious of, because
# three of the four rows were FAILING at 3 and pass at 4. The reason to believe
# it anyway is the fourth: RB28R returned 3 and passed against the wrong label,
# and at the corrected label it FAILS. Correcting the count converted a false
# pass into a real under-split, which tuning-to-pass cannot do.
# It also exposes what this column cannot see. RB30C's four rows are the right
# NUMBER and the wrong BOUNDARIES -- it cuts "I picked up the blood work
# results" away from "the iron is low again", then fuses that finding to the
# errand it caused. A count metric scores that identical to a correct split.
# Boundary correctness needs its own column; until it has one, do not read a
# passing count on a four-way split as evidence the split was right.
# RB14 is a known-bad row, kept and labelled rather than deleted. "give
# Dimitri the blue chair" routes to Memory because `give` is not in
# ActionabilityReader.actionVerb and the shape rule cannot see past the
# recipient to the determiner. Checked against 3,020 readable utterances: every
# other double-object dative in the corpus uses a verb already on the list
# (tell, text, email, send, remind), so the only capture this costs is the one
# I wrote. It measures a vocabulary boundary, not how anyone rambles, and its
# twin gap is 0 -- both halves fail identically. Do not fix the parser for it.
